Source: @darvishnameh

💧 Environmental water rights: from allocation on paper to water reaching the wetland

The report "Regulatory Oversight of Environmental Water Rights Allocation under Table (7) of Article (37) of the Seventh Development Plan Law," prepared by Mehdi Rajabi and Ali Haji-Moradi in Shahrivar 1405, examines the gap between legal commitments and the actual delivery of water needed by ecosystems.

The report's findings for the water year 1403–1404 show that drought is not the only reason water rights are not being fulfilled; weaknesses in the allocation system, withdrawals along the route, lack of coordination among agencies, and the absence of transparent monitoring also play a role.

The report's central message is clear: releasing water from a dam alone does not mean environmental water rights have been secured. The evaluation criterion must be whether water reaches the target ecosystem, in a volume, quality, and timing suited to its needs.

The report emphasizes reforming water allocation under water-scarce conditions, online monitoring and public disclosure of data, controlling withdrawals along the route, and integrated management of river basins.

🌱 Environmental water rights must hold a stable place in water allocation decisions — a share whose provision does not depend on water left over after other uses.

#Environmental_Water_Rights #Water_Governance #Wetlands #Seventh_Plan #Parliament_Research_Center

"We and Gazprom": A Documentary Account of Why Iran's Gas Industry Fell Behind

The second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast, titled "We and Gazprom," was screened today at the Atana Hotel in Tehran, attended by members of the Energy Commission of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, former and current energy officials, experts, and journalists. The documentary reviews Russia's experience in developing its gas industry to examine the obstacles facing the development of this industry in Iran and the role of Tehran-Moscow gas relations.

Focusing on the history of Russia's oil and gas industry, particularly the formation and expansion of the country's gas distribution network, the documentary seeks to examine the development paths of the gas industry in both Iran and Russia through the lens of historical experiences and strategic decisions.

In this episode, through conversations with veterans and experts of the gas industry, the question is raised: why has Iran, despite holding the world's second-largest natural gas reserves, been unable to develop its gas industry in proportion to its resource capacity and secure a more influential position in regional and global markets?

One of the documentary's central themes is the relationship between the abundance of gas resources, domestic pricing policy, and the development of gas industry infrastructure. Has the supply of cheap gas to consumers contributed to the sustainable development of this industry, or have pricing policies and rising domestic consumption constrained the resources needed for infrastructure investment and export development? The documentary seeks to examine various dimensions of this issue by presenting expert perspectives.

In another section, the documentary turns its attention to Iran-Russia gas relations—two countries that rank among the world's largest holders of natural gas reserves yet have taken different paths in developing gas exports. In this context, the question is raised: has Russia obstructed Iran's gas export development in recent years, and what impact has competition between the two countries had on Iran's export opportunities?

For fifteen years, they cut down the trees, slashed the bushes, displaced the animals, destroyed the birds' nests, and carved up the body of Mount Shahvar — this source of water, bread, and life for the people — and most of us just watched, without understanding what was being lost!

Some thought, what does one mountain matter? What harm could it do to take a piece of a mountain?

They didn't understand that Shahvar is not just stone, not just a home for bears, not just a shelter for birds, not just the memory of the forest — but a part of the life cycle on which the life of the plains, agriculture, and the people of Bastam and Shahroud depend, to which they are bound.

Those who saw the stone but not the water, who saw the mine but not the land. Those who failed to understand that the wound being inflicted today on the body of Mount Shahvar can tomorrow turn into the thirst of the earth, the pollution of water, and the endless suffering of the people — they must be held accountable today!

Now Shahvar remains; wounded and silent. A Shahvar that seems to have become a Shahzar for years, weeping bitterly to itself.

But it is no longer time for mourning alone. It is time to stand, time to ask, time to demand answers from those who allowed this wound to deepen every day for fifteen years!

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

Superadobe is an expanded method of the same old adobe, using long bags filled with moistened soil and then tamped down for proper compaction. The bags are stacked row by row in a circular plan, rising uniformly to form a dome. To prevent the bags from shifting and also to resist earthquakes, barbed wire is used between the layers, acting like mortar to bind the rows together and helping give the structure an integrated, chain-like quality that gives it high resistance to earthquakes and other events. In this structure, due to the dome form, the thickness of the walls, and the natural materials used, heat exchange with the outside is minimized and energy loss is managed dramatically. Superadobe was invented by Nader Khalili, an Iranian architect, and is now recognized worldwide as one of the methods for building sustainable and natural homes. 🔹 The festival, which focuses on environmental issues and the intersection of science, society, and documentary storytelling, will this year host works by environmental filmmakers and storytellers from around the world.

Filmed in Iran, Iraq, and Turkey, the documentary explores the issues of water, dam construction, oil development, and their environmental and human consequences.

🔹 Mohammad Darvish, environmental activist and researcher, narrates the documentary, which seeks to transcend political borders and paint a picture of the many factors that have shaped the fate of one of the region's most important wetlands.

🔹 The online section of the British Columbia Environmental Film Festival will run from November 1 to 30, 2026, and its in-person program will take place on November 22 at the University of British Columbia (UBC).

entry.summary:

Source: @darvishnameh

📝📝📝 The Shahnameh Becoming a Bestseller as a Sign of the Iranian People's Political Anxiety ✍️ Sina Jahanideh

✅ According to a report from one of the well-known publishers and bookstores, the best-selling book in Tehran's bookstores over the past few months has been Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Those with greater financial means have bought Jalal Khaleghi-Motlagh's multi-volume critical edition, while those with lower incomes have settled for the single-volume Shahnameh of the Moscow print.

✅ This is happening at a time when book prices have risen sharply, and even 250- or 300-page books sometimes reach around one million tomans; as a result, the era of the physical book is more exposed to decline than ever before. In the year 1405, it seems that buying books, compared to previous years, has become a difficult and unnecessary matter for a large part of society. Yet right in the middle of this very crisis, the Shahnameh has become a meaningful exception.

✅ Perhaps this phenomenon cannot be explained merely by literary interest or a growing desire to read the Shahnameh. For some buyers today, purchasing the Shahnameh has become a kind of cultural-political ritual rather than merely the purchase of a book; as if at a moment when Iran, for many people, is exposed to political, geographical, and identity anxieties, the Shahnameh has become something more than a literary text: a condensed symbol of "Iran."

✅ From this perspective, buying the Shahnameh is a kind of symbolic act; an act in which the individual feels that by taking the book home, they are also preserving something of Iran. In this situation, the Shahnameh is no longer just a book to read; it becomes an object that must be had, kept, and passed on to the next generation. This is why even under conditions of the collapse of the book economy, the purchase of the Shahnameh can increase.

✅ Here the Shahnameh is a metaphor for Iran, and buying it can be a symbolic response to the fear of Iran's loss. Therefore, perhaps the Shahnameh becoming a bestseller under such conditions can be seen not as a sign of increased reading of the Shahnameh, but as a sign of increased political and identity anxiety; an anxiety that manifests itself in the form of buying a book, or more precisely, in the form of buying a symbol.

✅ From this perspective, the Shahnameh in the current situation is not just a book; it is the last refuge of the fetish of the book: a place where the book, at the moment of the decline of book-reading, takes on the burden of something far greater than itself; the burden of Iran.
